messages.subject: Can mapreduce jobs be executed asynchronously?
messages.subject_clean: Can mapreduce jobs be executed asynchronously?
messages.body_plain:
Hi guys,

I'd like to know whether is possible to run mapreduce jobs in rmr in asynchronous fashion. When I run the mapreduce() function it always waits for the job to finish. We would like to put RHadoop into production and submit jobs over the Rook HTTP server, so that R submits the job and only returns ID or something.

Is this even something you had in mind when you were designing rmr? Or does it go out of the scope? Was RHadoop designed to be more of an improvement tool for people doing analytics on their local machines, instead of being plugged into an automatized production infrastructure? I don't want to bend RHadoop and force it into something it wasn't built for.

Am I overlooking something? How would you do this? (One possibility of course is to simply wait for the job to finish and Rook to return a HTTP response ...but that's kinda dirty)

messages.subject_clean: [RHadoop:#1247] Can mapreduce jobs be executed asynchronously?
messages.body_plain:
On Tue, Jan 7, 2014 at 4:06 AM, Daniel Kvasnička <daniel.kv...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi guys,
>
> I'd like to know whether is possible to run mapreduce jobs in rmr in asynchronous fashion.

Unfortunately, no.

> When I run the mapreduce() function it always waits for the job to finish. We would like to put RHadoop into production and submit jobs over the Rook HTTP server, so that R submits the job and only returns ID or something.
>
> Is this even something you had in mind when you were designing rmr? Or does it go out of the scope?

I think that's the main reason. If you can run asynchronously, you can run in parallel. The implications of that are wide ranging. Imagine you have

a = mapreduce(....);
a = mapreduce(....);

and mapreduce is called asynchronously. What is the semantics of this? What is the value of a at any given time?

> Was RHadoop designed to be more of an improvement tool for people doing analytics on their local machines, instead of being plugged into an automatized production infrastructure? I don't want to bend RHadoop and force it into something it wasn't built for.

I think RHadoop can be used for either as experience demonstrates, but it doesn't alone cover all the needs.

>
> Am I overlooking something? How would you do this? (One possibility of course is to simply wait for the job to finish and Rook to return a HTTP response ...but that's kinda dirty)

Take a look at this thread

http://r.789695.n4.nabble.com/running-R-commands-asynchronously-td3589434.html

The idea is to use one of the parallel computing packages, snow, foreach and related.

Antonio

Hi,
the TextInputFormat is for natural language, so that's not the correct choice. I would guess that a csv format is what you have in this case. Second, and offset in a file doesn't mean much in Hadoop since data sets are in general stored into multiple files, called parts, therefore the offset doesn't provide a total order, that is multiple records could have the same offset in different files. I would recommend adding a column with the row number, but the exact steps to achieve that are unclear from the information your provide, at least to me.

Antonio

I observed that each reducer took K / (# of reducers) duplicates. Now with YARN, it gave me errors about "Container is running beyond physical memory limits."
The strange thing is, it runs fine with K = K/10 or K = K/100. But would fail on the same setting except increase of K.

Container is running beyond physical memory limits. Current usage: 1.1 GB of 1 GB physical memory used; 2.0 GB of 2.1 GB virtual memory used.

yarn.nodemanager.resource.memory-mb = 20GB (24GB in total, reserve 4GB for system)

yarn.scheduler.minimum-allocation-mb = 1GB

yarn.scheduler.maximum-allocation-mb = 20GB

Is it because more resource cause more duplicate assigned to the container, which ends up with exceeding container capability. For instance, each matrix is 260MB in size, for a container of 1GB, 4 duplicates are assigned to container 1, but then results in an error.

I'm totally blind about how rmr2 works with YARN containers. Could anyone clarify? Many thanks in advance.

Sincerely,
Lishu

Hi,
first I have to admit I don't know the answer right away and I will investigate further. rmr2 doesn't directly access YARN and doesn't know anything about containers. rmr2 is using hadoop streaming which uses mapreduce which uses YARN. So you may be able to gather more information by searching for streaming and YARN and similar queries. Without more detail about your program is hard to guess why it would take more memory with more replication. If each replica is associated with a different key, the reducer need only load the data for one key at a time, unless there is a bug of course. One thing that I don't know and that could be of interest is whether the R process is included in the container. With streaming there are two processes for each task attempt: a java process and an R process. With mr1, from a memory management point of view, hadoop mapreduce ignored the R process. One had to make sure that the number of slots was small enough and the amount of memory allocated to the jvm small enough to leave room for R. With containers, this situation may have changed. There were some streaming bugs that prevented us from switching to mr2 for quite some time, so testing was impossible both internally and for our users. I am sure there will be some issues to iron out (even if all automated tests pass, but they cover only a number of use cases).

Antonio

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm testing rmr2 with the following setup:

- Hadoop 1.2.1, 5 nodes, each 3.7 GB RAM + 1 GB swap
- R 3.0.2
- latest versions of all the RHadoop packages
- a 1.6 GB CSV file that contains exactly 1 million rows with 40 columns (this is only a test file - we plan to go up to 100 million rows)

The mapper fn is as follows:

function(k, r) {
    r$ppdm <- r[[idx1]] / r[[idx2]]
    keyval(r[[splitter]], r)
}

Basically, I need to compute a value for every row, add it to the row and return the data with hadoop key being one of the values from the row. There are about 75.000 distinct values in the splitter column.
When I run the job Hadoop decides to use 25 mappers, which means that 40.000 rows should be processed by one mapper - which is nothing for both Java and R and should be pretty quick IMHO.
But the R processes on all 5 nodes that run the first 5 maps (with 20 pending) behave exactly the same way - they slowly eat more than 3 GB or physical memory and are then killed by Linux OOM killer. The Hadoop job retries a bunch of times and then finally dies. The same for a 500.000 rows dataset.
When I run the same in local mode with only 100.000 rows I get the same problem - the R proces goes well north of 3 GB of RAM and is beheaded.
The same thing with 30 rows of data works exactly as it should.
The Hadoop & R setup is OK and works well for other types of algorithms I've tried.

Do you have any idea what's wrong?

messages.subject: Re: Data frame from HBase scan
messages.body_plain:
I took a closer look at your code, and would recommend a change so you can support both scans on a specific set of columns and on an entire column family (see below)

#create a dataframe from a scan
hb.scan.data.frame <- function( tablename, startrow, end=NULL, colspec,sz=hb.defaults("sz"), usz=hb.defaults("usz"),
                                hbc=hb.defaults("hbc") )
{
  scn <- hb.scan( tablename, startrow, end, colspec, sz, usz, hbc )
  f <- scn$get()
  get_column_index_values <- function( column_index )
  {
    get_value <- function( row, column_name )
    {
      indices <- which( row[[ 2 ]] == column_name )
      index <- ifelse( length( indices ) == 1, indices[[ 1 ]], 0 )
      ifelse( index == 0, NA, row[[ 3 ]][[ index ]] )
    }
    column_name <- cols[[ column_index ]]
    unlist( lapply( f, get_value, column_name ) )
  }
  #get the vector of columns from the first row
  cols<-f[[1]][[2]]
  df <- as.data.frame( lapply( 1:length(cols), get_column_index_values ) )
  rownames( df ) <- unlist( lapply( f, "[[", 1 ) )
  colnames( df ) <- cols
  df
}

cols <- ifelse( length( colspec ) == 1, f[[ 1 ]][[ 2 ]], colspec )
